questions.q: In the line "dkx”k dk ,d iUuk] dksbZ vaèkM+ dgha ls vk;k {k.k dk cht ogk¡ cks;k x;k", identify the figure of speech (alankar) operating in "dkx”k dk iUuk" and name the two terms being compared.
questions.a: The figure of speech is **Rupak Alankar (Metaphor)** where "dkx”k" (head) is the *upameya* (subject) and "iUuk" (map) is the *upamana* (vehicle); the comparison is implicit without "jaise" or "sa". A wrong answer naming "Upama (Simile)" reveals the student misses the absence of comparative particles and treats all comparisons as explicit.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the phrase "'kCn osQ vaoqQj iwQVs] iYyo&iq"iksa ls ufer gqvk fo'ks"k" uses syntactic inversion and lexical compression to convey the creative process.
questions.a: Standard prose order would be "'kCnksa dh vaoqQj iwQV jati hai aur iYyo-iq"iksa se fo'ks"k ufer hota hai"; the poem front-loads the object "'kCn osQ vaoqQj" and uses the compound "iYyo&iq"iksa" (form-meaning) as a single compressed unit, mimicking the sudden unlocking of meaning. A student who merely paraphrases without noting the fronting and compounding misses how syntax *enacts* the poetic insight.

questions.q: Apply the concept of *chitrit abhivyakti* (pictorial expression) to the second poem: quote one visual image and one auditory image from "cxqyksa d ia[k", then explain how the grammatical form of each (noun phrase vs. verb phrase) shapes the sensory mode.
questions.a: Visual: "dtjkjs cknyksa dh NkbZ uHk Nk;k" (noun phrase "NkbZ uHk" — static, spatial). Auditory: "rSjrh lk¡> dh lrst 'osr dk;k" (verb phrase "dk;k" — dynamic, temporal). Noun phrases freeze the image; verb phrases release sound into time. A wrong answer that lists images without grammatical categorisation shows inability to link form to sensory effect.

questions.q: Compare the use of personification in both poems: in "NksVk esjk [ksr" the map "cks;k x;k" (was drawn) and "cht xy x;k" (the dot spread), while in "cxqyksa d ia[k" the wings "tkrh eq>s ck¡èk fut ek;k ls" (seem to fly toward me). Analyse how agency is distributed differently.
questions.a: In the first poem, inanimate objects (map, dot) *receive* action passively ("cks;k x;k", "xy x;k" — passive/ergative), suggesting the mind as a surface acted upon. In the second, the wings *initiate* motion ("tkrh" — active intransitive), granting nature autonomous agency. A student who only spots "personification" in both misses the shift from passive reception to active volition, which mirrors the thematic shift from introspection to outward connection.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The poet's use of Tatsam-heavy vocabulary (e.g., 'vaèkM+', 'cht', 'fo'ks"k', 'vk'k;', 'HkkoukRed') creates intellectual distance, while Tadbhav/Deshaj words (e.g., 'pkSdksuk', 'Nk;k', 'ck¡èk', 'fut') restore intimacy." Defend or refute with evidence from either poem.
questions.a: The claim is **partially valid but oversimplified**. "vaèkM+" (storm) and "cht" (dot) are Tatsam yet denote raw, visceral forces — no distance. Conversely, "pkSdksuk" (scaffold/platform) is Tadbhav but functions as a structural metaphor, not intimate speech. The real pattern: *abstract nouns* tend toward Tatsam ("fo'ks"k", "HkkoukRed"), *concrete sensory nouns* toward Tadbhav/Deshaj ("Nk;k", "ck¡èk"). A student who accepts the binary without checking each word's semantic field reveals a vocabulary-classification misconception.

questions.q: Write four original lines in Hindi that imitate the syntactic pattern of "jl dk v{k; ik=k lnk dk / NksVk esjk [ksr pkSdksuk" — i.e., a genitive chain of three nouns ending in a metaphorical noun — to describe a personal object (e.g., your phone, notebook, bicycle).
questions.a: Example: "smartphone dk skreen / duniya dk darvaza / meri jeb ka jagat" (screen of smartphone / door of world / universe of my pocket). A strong answer maintains the [Noun1 ka/ke/ki Noun2] ×2 → [Metaphorical Noun] structure and yields a fresh insight. A weak answer breaks the chain (e.g., uses adjectives instead of genitives) or produces a cliché ("dil ka darvaza"), showing inability to replicate the *generative* syntax.
